subject: history_social
passage: Before the 1880s, most American towns kept their own local time, set by the position of the sun, so that clocks in neighboring cities might differ by several minutes. For railroads coordinating hundreds of trains, the result was a tangle of conflicting timetables. On November 18, 1883, the major railroads of the United States and Canada simply adopted a system of standard time zones on their own. <u>The federal government did not make those zones law until 1918, some thirty-five years later.</u> That sequence complicates a familiar assumption about how standards come about: here, a private arrangement devised to solve a practical problem established the national rule that public authority later merely confirmed.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It states the central argument that the final sentence then illustrates with an example.
choices.B: It suggests that the railroads' time zones were unpopular until the government required them.
choices.C: It qualifies the claim that the railroads acted on their own by noting that they needed legal approval.
choices.D: It supplies a detail about timing that the author uses to challenge a common view of how standards arise.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence gives a date: the zones became law only in 1918, long after the railroads adopted them in 1883. The final sentence begins "That sequence complicates a familiar assumption," so the author uses this timing to argue that a private arrangement, not government action, set the standard.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The underlined sentence is a factual detail; the argument appears in the final sentence, which draws on that detail rather than illustrating it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the time zones were unpopular. The author's point is that the railroads' system already worked as the national rule.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The railroads did not need approval; the law came thirty-five years later and "merely confirmed" what they had done. This choice reverses the sentence's point.
explanation.D: Correct. The thirty-five-year gap is the evidence the author uses to challenge the assumption that standards begin with public authority.

checks.note: Best fit on the text alone.
